property_summary: After any call to addToBalance by an account funding the contract with a positive msg.value, the reference contract C increases that account's stored userBalance by exactly msg.value (so userBalance[actor] >= previous balance and increases by msg.value); the mutant that writes zero instead of adding will violate this (the balance will not increase) for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any deposit amount, after calling addToBalance with that amount the caller's recorded userBalance is at least as large as it was before the call (i.e., it increases by msg.value); the mutant that writes zero instead of adding can leave the caller's stored balance unchanged, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any two different addresses a (depositor) and k (observed key), depositing value v from a never decreases the stored balance of any other address k (i.e., userBalance(k) after deposit >= userBalance(k) before); the mutant that zeroes msg.value can leave other accounts' balances unchanged whereas the correct contract preserves/increases them when the deposit is to that same account, and crucially the mutant can violate non-decrease for the depositor when prior balance >0 if the implementation mistakenly subtracts — so we check non-decrease for an arbitrary (possibly distinct) observed key to expose the mutant.

For any depositor and any observed key, a call to addToBalance must never reduce the stored userBalance of that observed key (i.e., userBalance(k) after the deposit >= before); the mutant that writes zero instead of adding can make this non-decrease property fail for some inputs.

For every caller and value, calling addToBalance(x) on the reference always increases that caller's recorded userBalance by exactly x (i.e., userBalance(caller) after the call equals previous + x); removing the require allows a reentrant/recursive call during the modifier flow that can cause some address's userBalance to differ (be drained or not updated) for some inputs.

For every caller and any amount, a completed addToBalance call on the correct contract leaves some address's balance unchanged except increasing the caller's own stored balance by the sent amount (i.e., the call never triggers reentrant draining of other stored balances); the mutant that removes the require allows a reentrant attacker to drain or alter another user's stored balance during addToBalance, violating that invariant for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and deposit amount, a completed addToBalance call on the reference C never allows a malicious callee (that re-enters during the external call) to change another user's stored balance; removing the require enables a reentrant attacker to alter (drain) some victim's userBalance during addToBalance, so the invariant that victim's balance remains unchanged can be violated by the mutant.

For any depositor A, if A calls addToBalance sending value v while a separate attacker contract B is pre-funded and then (in its fallback/receive) attempts to re-enter addToBalance on behalf of some victim V, the correct contract C preserves the invariant that the total sum of all userBalance entries equals the cumulative deposits made so far (i.e., contract accounting is consistent), whereas the mutant that removes the require can break this conservation (total stored userBalance can decrease) by enabling a reentrant sequence that withdraws or corrupts other balances.

For any depositor A and any deposit amount v, after A calls addToBalance with value v the contract's total ether balance (address(c).balance) equals the sum of all stored userBalance values (i.e., accounting is conserved); removing the require enables a reentrant attacker to withdraw funds during addToBalance and break this conservation for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero deposit amount, after calling addToBalance() the contract's recorded user balance for that caller increases by exactly the sent value (so getBalance(addr) == previous + value); the mutant that omits updating the mapping breaks this because the stored balance does not increase for some inputs (e.g., any positive value).

After a successful addToBalance call by any user with any nonzero value, that user's stored balance in C equals the sum of prior balance and the sent value (reference preserves this invariant by non-reentrancy; the mutant removing the lock can be exploited by a reentrant attacker to cause inconsistency), and the test finds a reentrant sequence that breaks this for some inputs.

Rule: After any single call to addToBalance by an honest externally-owned user (EOA), the contract's stored userBalance for that EOA equals the sent value; the mutant without reentrancy protection can be exploited by a reentrant attacker contract calling back during addToBalance to make the stored balance be less than the sent value for some fuzzed amounts, breaking the rule.

For any caller and any payment amount, a single atomic call to addToBalance must increase that caller's stored userBalance by exactly the sent value (i.e. after addToBalance returns, getBalance(caller) == priorBalance + amount) in the reference via non-reentrancy; the mutant removing the lock allows a reentrant attacker (a helper contract) to call back during addToBalance and cause the stored balance to differ for some fuzzed amounts and attacker addresses.

Invariant: For any caller and any payment amount, if the caller is an attacker contract whose receive() re-enters withdrawBalance during addToBalance, then in the correct contract after addToBalance returns the contract's ETH balance equals the sum of all userBalance entries (i.e., no ETH is drained by reentrancy); the mutant (removing the lock) allows the attacker to reenter and cause address(c).balance < sum of userBalance, violating that equality for some fuzzed amount and attacker address.

For any attacker contract address and any nonzero fuzzed deposit amount, calling addToBalance from a reentrant attacker must NOT increase the attacker's recorded userBalance by more than the amount actually sent (reference enforces this by nonReentrant; the mutant without the lock can reenter and manipulate internal state so recorded balance becomes larger than sent for some inputs).

For any caller and deposit amount, after calling withdrawBalance the contract's balance is reduced by exactly the caller's withdrawn amount (i.e., address(c).balance == prior_balance - withdrawn_amount); the buggy mutant that zeroes the user balance before sending can be re-entered to withdraw more, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any depositor and deposit amount, if a malicious recipient reverts during the external send in withdrawBalance then the reference C leaves the depositor's recorded balance unchanged (still the deposited amount) because the call reverts and entire withdrawBalance reverts; the mutant that zeros the balance before the external call would instead set the recorded balance to 0 even though the external call reverted, so the mutant violates this property for some inputs.

For any depositor and deposit amount, if a re-entrant attacker drains the contract by reentering during withdrawBalance(), the reference implementation ensures the depositor's recorded balance is zero after successful withdrawal (because funds were sent before zeroing in the reference), while the mutant that zeroes before the external call can cause a different final recorded balance for the depositor when the external call reenters and manipulates balances.

For any depositor and any attacker contract address, if the depositor funds C and then the depositor (or an attacker contract) calls withdrawBalance, then after a successful withdrawBalance call the depositor's recorded balance in C is equal to 0; the mutant that zeros before the external call can be re-entered by an attacker to cause withdrawBalance to complete successfully while leaving the depositor's recorded balance non-zero for some inputs (attacker contracts).

For any depositor and any non-reentrant attacker contract address, if the depositor funds C and then that attacker calls withdrawBalance, then in the correct contract the depositor's recorded balance remains 0 after a successful withdraw (the call sends the stored funds and then zeroes the balance), while the mutant that zeros the balance before sending can allow reentrancy to make the final stored balance non-zero for some inputs (attacker reentering).

Invariant: after calling withdrawBalance() the caller's stored userBalance is set to zero (no funds remain credited); removing the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to reenter withdrawBalance and drain more than their credited balance so this invariant can be violated.

For any attacker-deposited amount, a single call to withdrawBalance() on the correct contract empties only the attacker’s recorded balance (address(c).balance decreases by that amount and c.getBalance(attacker) == 0 after the call); the mutant without the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to withdraw more than its recorded balance so this property can be violated for some deposit amount and attacker.

For any attacker address and deposit amount, a single external call to withdrawBalance() from a non-contract EOA or from a contract that does NOT reenter must leave C's total contract balance equal to the pre-withdraw balance minus at most the attacker's recorded balance and must not decrease by more than the attacker's recorded balance; the mutant (with disabled lock) can be drained via a reentrant attacker contract causing address(c).balance to drop by more than the attacker's recorded balance in one withdraw call.

For any attacker-deposited amount and attacker contract that reenters, a single call to withdrawBalance() on the correct contract will not make address(c).balance decrease by more than the attacker's recorded balance before the call (i.e., the contract cannot be drained for more than the caller's balance in one withdraw), whereas the mutant with the lock disabled can be reentered to withdraw more than its recorded balance and thus reduce address(c).balance by more than that recorded balance for some inputs.

For every attacker-deposited amount and an attacker contract that reenters during withdraw, a single call to withdrawBalance() on the correct contract C will leave C.getBalance(attacker) == 0 after the call (the recorded balance is set to zero exactly once), whereas the mutant with the reentrancy lock disabled can end up with C.getBalance(attacker) > 0 after the call because reentrant withdrawals can observe and manipulate balance flow causing the final stored balance to differ for some inputs.

After a successful withdrawBalance call by any user, their stored userBalance must be zero (reference enforces zeroing after safe external send); the mutant can leave a non-zero balance because it sets the reentrancy lock only after the call returns, allowing reentrancy to re-deposit and cause the final stored balance to be non-zero.

Invariant: after any call to withdrawBalance by an address that had a positive balance and where the external call target forwards control back (reentrant attacker), the user's stored balance in the correct contract is zero, but the mutant allowing reentrancy during execution can leave the balance non-zero for some inputs (attacker reenters during the external call and deposits again).

For any caller and deposit amount, if an address with a positive balance calls withdrawBalance and the external recipient REVERTS during the external call, the reference contract leaves the caller's recorded userBalance unchanged (still positive) because the external transfer failed and the balance reset happens only after a successful external send; the mutant that moves the lock after _ allows reentrancy during the send and can end with a different final userBalance for some inputs (the mutant can end with zero or other unexpected values when the external call reenters).

For any caller and any nonzero deposit, after the caller successfully calls withdrawBalance the contract's ETH balance must be strictly less than it was before the call (the reference releases the caller's funds exactly once), whereas the mutant that sets the reentrancy lock only after the body can be reentered during the external call and may finish with the contract still holding the withdrawn funds (so the contract balance does not decrease) for some attacker behavior.

For any depositor and any attacker-deployed reentrant helper, if the depositor funds C then the depositor's balance after calling withdrawBalance (which performs an external call to msg.sender) is always zero in the correct contract; the mutant that enables reentrancy during the external call can cause the depositor's getter to be non-zero after withdraw for some attacker behavior and deposit amounts.

For any caller and any pre-funded balance, after a successful withdrawBalance call the contract's stored userBalance for every account remains zero (reference preserves clearing of the caller's balance before/after transfer semantics), whereas the mutant that moves the zeroing can leave non-caller balances unchanged in ways that differ for some inputs (specifically a reentrant attacker can cause balances to differ).

For any caller and attacker address and any deposit amounts, when an attacker re-enters during withdraw, the reference C always leaves every user's balance equal to 0 after withdrawBalance completes; the mutant that zeroes after the external call can leave the attacker’s balance non-zero (so the property is violated for some inputs).

For any depositor and any attacker who may reenter, after calling withdrawBalance by the depositor the reference C always ensures the depositor's userBalance is zero (no funds remain recorded) for all inputs; the mutant that zeroes after the external call can leave the depositor's balance non-zero when a reentrant attacker causes extra transfers, so the property is violated for some inputs.
